explanations.explanation: This feature detects word-final affix sequences—common morphological suffixes (case endings in Finnish, verb-plural or derivational endings in other languages)—i.e. it lights up on the letter patterns that signal an inflectional or derivational suffix attached to a stem.
This neuron specializes in recognizing the boilerplate legal header you find atop source files—copyright notices, “licensed under…” clauses, warranty disclaimers, URLs to the license text, etc.
This neuron detects binary‐link markers—words like “to” in ranges (X to Y) or “or” in alternatives (X or Y)—that join two comparable items or endpoints.

This feature acts as a “relational‐marker” detector, firing on tokens that introduce or mark comparisons, subordination or categorical/hierarchical relations—whether syntactically (comparative markers like “than,” prepositions like “over,” relative pronouns “who”/“that”), or morphologically (hierarchy prefixes “sub-,” “super-,” “inferior,” and domain‐specific suffixes like “-ase,” “-lect,” “-ped”).

explanations.explanation: This neuron is essentially a “word‐ending” detector—it lights up on subword tokens that form common morphological or name suffixes (–man, –ism, –house, –ence, etc.) rather than on roots or prefixes.
This neuron detects section- or topic-boundary markers—tokens that signal a shift or new segment in the text (e.g. the discourse transition “in any case,” forum breaklines, or formal legal headings).

This feature fires on the standard “preamble” or header block of a legal-opinion (or similar) document — the line(s) that give the official citation (volume, reporter, page, year), the court name/division, docket or case number, date, parties (“v.”), and counsel. It also generalizes to similarly structured metadata headers (e.g. HTML head tags), marking the transition from document metadata into the body.
This feature picks out the little markup tokens that encode document structure in scientific texts—things like section‐ID anchors (“{#s1}”) and citation/reference keys (“[@…B19]”, “R1”, etc.).
